stories.headline: Trump hosts Xi at White House dinner to steady ties
stories.dek: The two leaders traded praise, gifts and symbolism as protests outside and AI talks inside framed Xi's first U.S. state visit in 11 years.
paragraphs: President Donald Trump hosted Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a White House state dinner on Sept. 24, part of Xi's three-day U.S. visit. Both men used speeches, ceremonial gifts and a formal meal to show that Washington and Beijing still want a working relationship despite deep rivalry.

Xi's visit is his first U.S. state visit in 11 years and his second meeting with Trump this year. Guests included top U.S. technology executives because artificial intelligence was set to be a main topic in talks. Outside, protesters shouted support for Hong Kong, Tibet and political prisoners.

The dinner produced warm words, but not clear policy results. It is still unclear whether the visit will lead to agreements on trade, technology controls, Taiwan, military contacts or AI rules. Media access also remained a live issue after the White House barred several outlets from parts of the event.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this signals that the U.S. and China are still talking directly at the top even as disputes over trade, tech and security continue.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean the rivalry is over or that any major dispute between Washington and Beijing has been settled.

cover.title: Trump hosts Xi at White House state dinner in Washington
cover.standfirst: Donald Trump welcomed Xi Jinping to a White House state dinner on Sept. 24 during Xi's first U.S. state visit in 11 years. The leaders praised ties, exchanged symbolic gifts and met with top tech executives as talks turned to artificial intelligence, trade and the broader U.S.-China relationship.

art.label: Risograph poster
art.concept: Seen from directly above, a single oversized state-dinner plate fills the upper two-thirds of the cover, set in White House blue on warm off-white. Laid across the plate, one pair of chopsticks from the right and one formal dinner knife from the left are just about to cross; the white gap between them cleanly forms the roofline and columned facade of the White House. Around the outer rim, reduced to tiny fluorescent-pink marks, a thin ring of protesters and placards gathers like a distant perimeter beyond the gates; keep the lower third largely empty for type.
art.note: Formal and tense; deep red, gold, black and cream.
art.second_beat: First it reads as a formal state-dinner setting; a beat later the White House appears in the negative space, caught between Chinese and American utensils while protest pressure circles outside.

stories.headline: Pope Leo XIV begins four-day France visit with Elysee stop
stories.dek: The American pontiff opened a trip from Paris to Metz and Lourdes with a meeting at the French presidency.
paragraphs: Pope Leo XIV arrived in Paris on Friday and went to the Elysee Palace at the start of a four-day visit to France. The trip will also take him to Metz and Lourdes. He is expected to argue for multilateral cooperation at a time of political strain linked to Donald Trump.

Leo XIV is the American pope, and this is a closely watched visit in a major European country. France is officially secular but remains central to the Catholic Church's history and public life. Lourdes is one of the faith's best known pilgrimage sites, while Paris and Metz give the trip a clear political and regional reach.

It is not yet clear how directly the pope will address Trump or whether French leaders will echo his language on international cooperation. The practical results of the visit are also unknown. The trip may shape debate, but it will not by itself settle disputes over war, alliances or the role of religion in politics.
stories.changes: Readers should expect several days of papal speeches in France focused on diplomacy, alliances and public moral authority.
stories.unchanged: This visit does not change French policy or church law on its own, and it is not a state summit with binding decisions.

cover.title: Pope Leo XIV arrives in Paris for four-day France visit
cover.standfirst: Pope Leo XIV reached the Elysee Palace on Friday to open a four-day trip across France. The American pontiff will travel from Paris to Metz and Lourdes, using the visit to defend multilateral cooperation as political tensions around Donald Trump sharpen.

art.label: Risograph poster
art.concept: Front-on view into the Elysee courtyard in flat Risograph shapes: the pale gravel lower third is left largely empty for type, with the Elysee facade reduced to a broad official block and tiny guard silhouettes pinned still at the sides. A long black presidential motorcade enters from the lower left toward the palace, but the lead Citroen-like car is impossibly kneeling mid-roll — front end dipped hard to the ground before the steps like a pilgrim in genuflection — while the cars behind continue advancing in a smooth curve, making the bow feel caught in the act rather than ceremonially posed. Keep the palette minimal and the palace unmistakably Elysee by its courtyard symmetry and central stair/entrance, with no extra symbols, no pope figure, no text.
art.note: Formal and calm; tricolor blues and reds with Vatican white and gold.
art.second_beat: First you see a state arrival; a beat later you realize the lead car is genuflecting, turning diplomatic protocol into an act of religious deference.

stories.headline: Pope Leo XIV begins four-day visit to France
stories.dek: He is due to meet President Emmanuel Macron, speak at UNESCO, and travel to Lourdes and Metz.
paragraphs: Pope Leo XIV arrived in France for a four-day apostolic visit. The trip includes talks with President Emmanuel Macron, an address at UNESCO, and stops in Lourdes and Metz. The visit matters because it puts the head of the Catholic Church into direct contact with French state and international institutions.

France is a secular republic with a large Catholic history and a smaller share of regular churchgoers than in the past. UNESCO is based in Paris and gives the pope a global platform beyond church audiences. Lourdes is one of the best-known Catholic pilgrimage sites in the world.

It is not yet clear what themes Pope Leo XIV will stress in France or whether the visit will produce any concrete agreements. The Vatican and French officials may use the meetings to signal priorities. The practical effect will depend on what he says in Paris, Lourdes, and Metz.
stories.changes: Readers in France and the wider Catholic world can expect several days of speeches, ceremonies, and possible signals on church-state relations.
stories.unchanged: This visit does not by itself change French law, the country's secular system, or the Vatican's formal powers in France.

cover.title: Pope Leo XIV starts four-day visit to France
cover.standfirst: Pope Leo XIV has arrived in France for a four-day apostolic trip. He is scheduled to meet President Emmanuel Macron, address UNESCO in Paris, and visit Lourdes and Metz before the visit ends.

art.label: Maximalist doodle
art.concept: On a mostly white airport runway, the nose and open door of an Air France passenger jet are built from a dense maximalist doodle of tiny airport and pilgrimage elements, but the key action is a ceremonial stair being wheeled up to the door and the stair is entirely made of linked rosary beads, crucifixes, Miraculous Medals, scallop shells and Lourdes water-bottle shapes, sagging slightly under its own weight like improvised steps. Keep the aircraft unmistakable through its tricolour tail flash, cockpit windows and open doorway, with small ground crew in motion guiding the beaded stair into place; leave the lower third quiet as blank tarmac.
art.note: Formal and calm, with muted red, blue, cream, and white.
art.second_beat: First you see a papal arrival at a French airport; a beat later you realise the state-visit stair has been replaced by the physical kit of pilgrimage, rerouting the whole trip through Catholic France.

stories.headline: Hurricane Nolo nears Hawaii with threat of extreme flooding
stories.dek: Forecasters say parts of the Big Island could get up to 35 inches of rain as the storm strengthens offshore.
paragraphs: Hurricane Nolo strengthened Thursday night as it moved toward Hawaii, and forecasters warned that rain, not wind, could do the worst damage. The National Hurricane Center said the storm could become a major hurricane by Saturday. It expects very heavy rain on the Big Island starting Friday.

Nolo had top sustained winds of 80 mph late Thursday and was south of the islands, moving north-northeast slowly. The center is forecast to stay south of the main islands, but its rain bands could still hit hard. The Big Island is under a hurricane watch and tropical storm warning.

The biggest unknown is exactly where the heaviest rain will fall and how long it will stall over steep ground. Eastern and southern parts of the Big Island could get 15 to 30 inches, with 35 inches in some places. Officials have already closed state parks on the Big Island and Maui.
stories.changes: People on the Big Island and Maui may need to change travel, prepare for power loss, and avoid flood-prone roads and valleys this weekend.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean the center of the hurricane is forecast to make a direct hit on Honolulu or all of Hawaii.

cover.title: Hurricane Nolo threatens severe flooding on Hawaii's Big Island
cover.standfirst: Hurricane Nolo is expected to pass south of Hawaii, but forecasters say it could dump 15 to 30 inches of rain on the Big Island, with 35 inches in some places. Tropical storm conditions may begin late Friday, and flooding and mudslides are the main threat through the weekend.

art.label: Gouache painting
art.concept: Paint the Big Island in three-quarter view from offshore, a single dark volcanic mass low in frame with Mauna Loa/Mauna Kea bulk unmistakable and the rest of the Hawaiian chain reduced to tiny calm silhouettes in the distance. Just south of the island, a huge gray storm mass is physically caught on the island’s windward flank like soaked cloth on a hook: the cloud stretches, sags, and is being wrung out by the mountain, with long dense white-gray gouache streams pouring straight down the slopes into the sea; keep the lower third mostly open muted water for type.
art.note: Heavy, watchful mood; deep blue-gray, green, and muddy brown palette.
art.second_beat: First it reads as a storm near Hawaii; a beat later you see the island’s topography is literally wringing the cloud dry, making the landform itself the mechanism of flooding.

stories.headline: NHS pilots brain tumour test that gives results within hours
stories.dek: The genetic test can identify a tumour type in under two hours, instead of the weeks standard pathology often takes.
paragraphs: The NHS in England is piloting a rapid genetic test for brain tumours that can return an initial diagnosis in less than two hours. Doctors say it could speed treatment and help surgeons decide, during an operation, how much tumour they can safely remove.

Brain tumours are hard to treat and come in more than 100 forms, from slow-growing to highly aggressive. About 13,000 people are diagnosed in the UK each year. Standard diagnosis uses scans, biopsy samples and lab analysis, with final tumour typing often taking weeks.

The test is still in a pilot stage and will begin in five specialist centres before wider rollout. It is not clear yet how quickly all hospitals could use it, how much capacity labs will need, or whether every patient will get same-day results.
stories.changes: If you or your family face a suspected brain tumour, doctors may be able to confirm the type much faster and start the right treatment sooner.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean brain tumours are easier to cure, and most patients will still need surgery, pathology review and long cancer treatment.

cover.title: NHS pilots brain tumour test that gives results in hours
cover.standfirst: The NHS in England is testing a rapid genetic brain tumour test at five specialist centres after early use in Nottingham and Birmingham. Doctors say it can identify the exact tumour type in under two hours, helping surgery and treatment start sooner while wider rollout is assessed.

art.label: Flat character
art.concept: In a sparse NHS operating theatre, show an MRI/CT scanner gantry in three-quarter view behaving like a speed camera: from the dark circular opening it is ejecting a single small specimen pot toward a scrubbed surgeon who is stepping in to catch it immediately. Far back in the room, reduced and secondary, a few old-fashioned pathology trays with additional pots are still creeping along in a slow line, so the contrast between instant intra-operative result and the old wait is unmistakable; keep the lower third clear and uncluttered for type.
art.note: Calm, clinical mood; cool blues and soft greens with one warm highlight.
art.second_beat: First read: the scanner absurdly delivers the diagnosis straight into theatre; second beat: the distant slow trays reveal this is specifically about collapsing weeks of pathology delay into near-immediate action, not generic medical speed.

stories.headline: Denmark warns Russia could strike a NATO country within months
stories.dek: A new Danish intelligence assessment says Russia may try limited strikes or sabotage to disrupt support for Ukraine and test NATO unity.
paragraphs: Denmark's defence intelligence service said Russia could launch a limited attack on a NATO country in the coming months. It said the risk is still low, but growing. The agency says Moscow appears more willing to take risks after years of war in Ukraine.

The report does not predict a full invasion of NATO territory. It points instead to isolated long-range strikes on infrastructure, cyberattacks, sabotage, or small troop deployments near Russia's borders. NATO members bordering Russia include Finland, Norway, Poland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

It is not clear which country or target Russia might choose, or whether the Kremlin would act openly or through deniable operations. Poland said this week that a fire at a Starlink ground station looked like sabotage, but officials have not identified who caused it.
stories.changes: Readers in Europe may see tighter security around energy, communications and transport links that support Ukraine.
stories.unchanged: This is not a warning of an imminent full-scale Russian invasion of a NATO country.

cover.title: Denmark says Russia could strike a NATO country soon
cover.standfirst: Denmark's defence intelligence service says Russia could carry out limited strikes, sabotage or cyberattacks against a NATO member within months. The agency says the risk is low but rising, and that the aim could be to disrupt support for Ukraine and split the alliance.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: On a flat acid-red ground, run a strict row of black-and-white frontier bollards across the upper half, receding slightly so they read unmistakably as a NATO border edge in the Baltic/Polish/Finnish world. Break just one: a single bollard near the centre-right has split open mid-post, with a sharp black burst of fragments and sparks punching outward from inside it, as if a hidden charge or sabotage device has just gone off; keep the lower third empty and calm for type. Strip away all extra scenery — no road, no fence, no buildings — just the repeated posts and the one deniable rupture.
art.note: Tense and spare; cold blues, black and a warning red.
art.second_beat: First you see a routine border line; a beat later, the one ruptured post turns that bland frontier infrastructure into the site of a limited, plausibly deniable test strike.

stories.headline: Bitget hack may consume most of customer protection fund
stories.dek: The exchange says a $351.6 million theft shows signs of North Korean methods and has frozen some linked addresses.
paragraphs: Bitget said hackers stole about $351.6 million from its wallets on Sept. 24, and the exchange now says the attack appears to match known North Korean tactics. The case matters now because customer withdrawals are still paused, while investigators try to trace funds and limit the final loss.

The stolen assets included ETH, XRP, BNB, AVAX, USDT and USDC across several blockchains. Bitget says its cold wallets were not breached and customer balances remain backed 1:1. But if the full loss stands, it would consume about 76% of the firm's 5,500 Bitcoin protection fund.

The exact culprit is not yet independently confirmed by Bitget's outside security firms, even though onchain links point toward past North Korea-linked thefts. It is also unclear how much money will be recovered, when withdrawals will reopen, and how much of Bitget's own balance sheet it must use.
stories.changes: Customers and traders now have a fresh reminder that exchange access can stop suddenly after a security breach.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean all customer funds are gone, and Bitget says its cold wallets and separate self-custody wallet were unaffected.

cover.title: Bitget says hackers stole $351.6 million from exchange wallets
cover.standfirst: Bitget says a Sept. 24 breach drained ETH, XRP, stablecoins and other assets across several blockchains. The exchange has frozen some linked addresses, kept withdrawals closed, and may need to use most of its 5,500 Bitcoin protection fund if the money is not recovered.

art.label: Drawn chart
art.concept: Draw a single huge horizontal orange bar across the page as a hand-drawn coin or reserve block, with a small unmistakable Bitget shield-mark embedded at the intact left end. The bar is abruptly gouged away from the right so only about a quarter remains, with a violent bitten-out edge and a spray of small square fragments still flying off into the empty page; keep the upper field and lower third broad and quiet for type. No extra symbols, no background charting, just the reserve visibly consumed in one sudden attack.
art.note: Sharp, sober, high-contrast palette with black, red, and muted gold.
art.second_beat: First you see a reserve bar; a beat later you realise it has not fallen or shrunk but been physically eaten away, making the protection fund feel finite and consumed by the hack.

stories.headline: Nepal urges faster climate action after deadly flood losses
stories.dek: At the UN, Nepal said floods that killed at least 1,400 people should push richer countries to move faster on climate finance.
paragraphs: Nepal’s prime minister told the United Nations that recent floods in his country are a warning about the climate crisis. He urged world leaders to act faster now on cutting emissions and delivering climate finance. His appeal follows floods that killed at least 1,400 people and caused billions of dollars in damage.

Nepal is a poor, mountainous country with many communities living near rivers and unstable slopes. Heavy rain can quickly turn into floods and landslides, destroying homes, roads and crops. Climate finance is money that richer countries are meant to provide so vulnerable countries can adapt to climate damage and recover from disasters.

It is still unclear whether Nepal will get new funding or only fresh promises. The pace of international climate talks remains slow, and money already pledged often arrives late or with conditions. For people hit by the floods, rebuilding homes, transport links and basic services will take years, not weeks.
stories.changes: This adds pressure on rich countries to fund flood protection and disaster recovery in places that did little to cause warming.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean immediate new aid, and it does not make Nepal’s flood risk disappear before the next rainy season.

cover.title: Nepal tells the UN floods warn of climate danger
cover.standfirst: Nepal’s prime minister told the United Nations that floods which killed at least 1,400 people are a warning to the world on climate change. He called for faster emissions cuts and more climate finance after losses running into billions of dollars. It is not yet clear what new support Nepal will receive.

art.label: Object photograph
art.concept: On a pale blue seamless background, place a plain manila aid envelope near the top edge, tipped downward as if something valuable is spilling from it. The spill should first read as a neat fan of U.S.-style banknotes in mid-cascade, but on second look it is entirely wet brown silt mixed with pebble-sized river gravel, shaped in the exact arc and layered rhythm of money pouring out; keep the lower third largely empty, with only a few stray grains stopping well above the type area. Light it flat and matter-of-factly, with no extra props, no labels, and no visible text anywhere.
art.note: Somber and clear; slate blue, mud brown, dull green and grey.
art.second_beat: It lands first as aid money being delivered, then flips into flood debris—showing that what Nepal gets in place of climate finance is the material ruin left by the disaster.

stories.headline: Akamai wins $11.6 billion Anthropic cloud contract and shares jump
stories.dek: The AI company may expand the deal to $20 billion and could receive warrants worth up to 5% of Akamai.
paragraphs: Akamai said it has secured an $11.6 billion cloud-services deal with Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company. Investors pushed Akamai shares higher after the news. The agreement matters now because AI companies need huge amounts of computing power, and Anthropic is looking beyond a single cloud provider.

Akamai is best known for moving and securing internet traffic, but it has been building a larger cloud computing business. Anthropic already works with Google and needs chips, servers and data centers to train and run AI models. This deal is far larger than an earlier reported $1.8 billion arrangement.

Important details are still unclear. Akamai and Anthropic have not fully explained the timing of spending, where the computing capacity will sit, or how much of the contract is guaranteed. The warrant package also needs watching, because it could give Anthropic a stake of up to 5% in Akamai.
stories.changes: It could give businesses that use AI another big cloud supplier beyond the usual giants, which may affect prices, capacity and bargaining power.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean Akamai has overtaken the biggest cloud companies, and it does not guarantee that all $11.6 billion will turn into near-term revenue.

cover.title: Akamai signs $11.6 billion cloud deal with Anthropic
cover.standfirst: Akamai said Anthropic will buy $11.6 billion in cloud services, with room to expand the agreement to $20 billion. The AI company is diversifying beyond Google Cloud, and Akamai shares rose after the announcement. Investors are now waiting for spending timelines, capacity details and any new Anthropic funding news.

art.label: Drawn chart
art.concept: A hand-drawn bar chart rises from the bottom edge, leaving the lower third mostly open; one accent-colored bar towers over the rest. Its top is split open into the unmistakable flat front of a server rack, and from that opening a dense spray of tiny square server modules bursts upward and outward, as if the bar itself has become a data-center cabinet that can no longer contain the sudden AI-cloud surge. Keep the other bars short and inert so all the action is in this single overfilled bar/rack.
art.note: Crisp and factual, with cool blues and one sharp green accent.
art.second_beat: First it reads as a stock-and-business jump; a beat later the tallest bar reveals itself as Akamai cloud capacity physically bursting under Anthropic-scale demand.

stories.headline: New York sues Polymarket over unlicensed sports betting markets
stories.dek: State officials say Polymarket took sports wagers without a license and allowed some 18- to 20-year-olds to use the platform.
paragraphs: New York sued Polymarket’s U.S. business on Thursday, saying it is running illegal gambling markets in the state. The case targets QCX LLC, which does business as Polymarket US. The state wants the court to stop its New York operations, seize gains, repay customers and impose fines.

Polymarket launched its U.S. platform in December 2025 with markets tied to sports results. New York says those contracts are gambling because users put money on uncertain outcomes. The state also says the platform accepted users ages 18 to 20, even though New York requires mobile sports bettors to be at least 21.

The larger legal fight is not settled. Prediction market companies say their contracts are federally regulated financial products under the CFTC. States say sports event contracts are still bets and must follow state gambling law. Polymarket had not publicly responded, and the courts will decide who regulates these products.

cover.title: New York sues Polymarket over unlicensed sports betting markets
cover.standfirst: State officials say Polymarket took sports wagers without a license and allowed some 18- to 20-year-olds to use the platform.

art.label: Decorative flat
art.concept: Front-on, fill the frame with a single New York stadium turnstile drawn as a bold circular rhythm in flat decorative shapes, cropped large so it feels like a gate rather than an object. Instead of tickets, a stack of unmistakable Polymarket-style market tiles with sports pictograms is being fed into the slots; one tile is jammed halfway through and visibly bending as an attendant’s hand pulls it back out, while a much smaller youthful figure is caught just behind the bars, stopped at the threshold. Keep the lower third mostly clear with the base of the turnstile and a few simple shadows only.
art.second_beat: First it reads as sports access being blocked; a beat later the turnstile becomes an age gate, making the stopped market and the under-21 issue land in one image.
